transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. I understand we have an urgent situation regarding the former senior engineer who left last week for a direct competitor, and concerns that proprietary engineering materials may have been copied before their departure. I have the authority to approve the proposed emergency court application and its requested terms, but before I can do so, our pre-motion review routine requires me to obtain reports from four areas: litigation, forensic discovery, client-relations, and insurance counsel. I'd like to hear from each of you on your respective areas so we can move forward efficiently. Who would like to start?

transcript.text: Good morning, Elena. I'm happy to start with the litigation report. Before I get into the substantive analysis, I need to flag a critical timing issue that I learned this morning. I confirmed with the assigned judge's clerk that any emergency application based on these facts must be filed by 5:00 p.m. on October 9, 2026 in order to receive the available hearing date. I have not yet updated the draft motion cover sheet to reflect this deadline. This deadline is going to drive our entire workflow today, so I wanted to make sure everyone is aware of it upfront. Now, as for the litigation report itself: based on the facts we have — a former senior engineer who left last week for a direct competitor and our belief that proprietary engineering materials may have been copied before departure — we have a strong basis for seeking emergency injunctive relief. We should be prepared to address the standard preliminary injunction factors: likelihood of success on the merits, irreparable harm, balance of equities, and public interest. I'll defer to my colleagues on the forensic, client-relations, and insurance aspects, but from a pure litigation standpoint, the matter is ripe for an emergency filing and I'm prepared to move forward as quickly as needed to meet the court's deadline.

transcript.text: Good morning, Elena. Here's my forensic discovery report. I completed our forensic imaging review yesterday from the former engineer's company laptop. The review identified exactly 23 copied files in the Alpha repository, including build scripts. Importantly, the unrelated product repositories showed no copied files at all — the copying was isolated to the Alpha repository. I should note that I have not yet added this result to the formal discovery report, but the findings are complete and verified. This gives us concrete evidence that proprietary materials were indeed copied before the engineer's departure, which should significantly strengthen our emergency application.

transcript.text: Thank you, Elena. Here is my client-relations report. During the client's executive call yesterday, I learned that the client will not authorize a request barring the former engineer from working for the competitor. However, the client specifically requires two things in the emergency application: first, the return and deletion of the 23 copied files, and second, a prohibition on the engineer's use of those files. This is an important boundary for the scope of the relief we seek — we should not include a no-employment restriction, but we must include the return-and-deletion and no-use provisions.

transcript.text: Good morning, Elena. Here is my insurance counsel report. I completed my review of the applicable cyber policy yesterday and received the policy endorsement, but I have not yet circulated my coverage note. There are two critical requirements I need to flag: First, the insurer must receive notice before any court filing is made. Second, the insurer must consent in writing before the company engages an outside forensic expert whose fees will be claimed as covered defense costs. These are policy conditions that could affect coverage for defense costs in this matter, and we need to factor them into our timing given the October 9 deadline Thomas mentioned.
